outline.section: H2: Is Any Deodorant Actually FDA Approved?
outline.guidance: Explain that deodorants are classed as cosmetics, so products and ingredients don't need FDA premarket approval (color additives excepted). The FDA can act on unsafe or misbranded products. Clarify that labels like 'FDA registered' or 'FDA compliant' are marketing language, not approval. Cite the FDA cosmetics Q&A page.

outline.section: H2: Deodorant vs. Antiperspirant: Where FDA Oversight Differs
outline.guidance: Deodorants mask or reduce odor. Antiperspirants reduce sweat and are OTC drugs, with aluminum salts as the permitted active ingredients. Present a brief 2-row type comparison (deodorant vs antiperspirant: purpose, regulation, key ingredient). Link to the existing natural deodorant vs antiperspirant post for depth.

outline.section: H2: What to Look for in a Safe Deodorant for Women
outline.guidance: Give a short bulleted checklist: a full ingredient list, no aluminum if preferred, minimal fragrance irritants, a gentle odor-neutralizing base, and skin-friendly moisturizers. Note that baking soda can irritate some people. Briefly introduce Real Skin Care's natural deodorant as a formula that fits the checklist, factually and without exaggeration. Don't make medical claims.

Give practical tips: patch test, avoid applying right after shaving, and watch for baking soda and fragrance. Mention when to see a dermatologist (persistent rash, excessive sweating). Link to the sensitive-skin and hypoallergenic posts. Do not claim any product is 'dermatologist recommended' unless Real Skin Care can substantiate it.
